item.title: How friends from Coimbatore built GOAT Robotics into an Rs 8 crore business with global reach
item.description: Coimbatore's GOAT Robotics grew from a 2BHK startup to an Rs 8 crore business, serving Toyota, Volvo and global clients.
item.content:encoded:
GOAT Robotics, a startup founded by friends who studied B.E. Robotics and Automation Engineering at a private engineering college in Coimbatore, a Tier 2 city, has achieved success by providing robotic services to several countries.

What began with a turnover of just Rs 10 lakh has now grown into a large company that spends Rs 40 lakh every month on salaries alone.

Muthu Vangaliappan, one of the Managing Directors and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of GOAT Robotics, shared the company's success story with us.

The nine founders of GOAT Robotics come from different districts, including Coimbatore, Erode, and Salem. All of them graduated in 2015 with a B.E. in Robotics and Automation Engineering from PSG Engineering College in Coimbatore. After securing jobs through campus placements, they moved to different companies across various states.

“During our college days, the nine of us were a close-knit group. We shared the same dream of studying well and achieving great heights in life. As time passed and we continued working, we began thinking about starting our own business. In 2015, Naveen, Dharmaraj, Mugesh, and I came together to establish a company called Katomaran Technologies Pvt. Ltd.,” said Muthu.

In the initial days, the four friends conducted seminars at colleges and provided robotics-related training to students and aspiring entrepreneurs.

To expand their business, they rented a 2BHK house in Coimbatore in 2018 and formally started operating Katomaran Technologies Pvt. Ltd. This beginning has now grown into a large company generating a turnover of more than Rs 8 crore.

Friends Who Started Their Journey Amid Severe Setbacks

Muthu says they faced several serious challenges and setbacks during the initial stages of their business before recovering.

“While we were providing automation and robotics services to small companies in India, we got an opportunity to work for a few companies in Singapore. We realised that there was always a shortage of around 40% of security personnel there. This led us to start using robotics and automation technology in the security sector.

“We made their work easier and addressed the manpower shortage by introducing various automation technologies, including automated toll gates and cameras, for people traffic, vehicle traffic, utility management, and surveillance. This project gave us good profits and valuable experience.

“We also began introducing robots in hotels. As the years passed, we started thinking about why we couldn't use the same technology in India. With that idea, in 2019, we continuously visited major hotels across India and submitted proposals for using robots,” Muthu shared, recalling the company's early days.

“However, we did not achieve the same level of success that we had experienced in Singapore. This was because the use of robots in India was very limited, and many people were unwilling to adopt them.

“While our business was doing well in Singapore, we faced setbacks when we shifted our focus to India.

Nevertheless, we continued working in hotels, not just with robots but also in areas such as 3D gaming and gaming simulators,” he said.

The Story Behind the Formation of GOAT Robotics

From 2019 to 2022, the team focused extensively on manufacturing specialised robots for hotels. They developed various robots, including room-service robots, hotel room-cleaning robots, bellboy robots, and dispensers, supplying them to five-star and seven-star hotels.

However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, they faced severe difficulties as they stopped receiving orders.

“While our business was progressing this way, five other friends who had studied with us were already running a company called Dotworld Technologies Pvt. Ltd.

“In 2023, their company and ours merged, and we established GOAT Robotics in Coimbatore. GOAT stands for Greatest of All Technologies,” he explained.

“When we started this company, we already had extensive experience in manufacturing, while the new group of friends had significant experience in marketing. Combining the expertise of both teams, we planned to provide automation and robotics-related services to major hotels in India.

“We frequently approached hotels and hospitals, conducted demonstrations, and submitted proposals. That was when we realised an important truth: this business model would work in foreign countries such as Singapore and Malaysia, but it would be difficult in India.

“We realised that we were running fast in the wrong direction. As we reached a point where we risked losing our business, we decided to develop a different category of robotics.”

They first began manufacturing and supplying lifting robots capable of carrying heavy loads. They developed robots for several companies to lift and move heavy objects. Later, they began manufacturing packing robots and providing automation solutions.

“We continued working with small companies through contracts. Within a few months, we received a good response. We then decided to pitch our idea to a major company for the first time.

“We sent our idea to Toyota, and they liked it and signed an agreement with us. Our journey with Toyota began in December 2023,” said Muthu.

From Coimbatore to Serving Countries Across the World

Muthu shared that getting an opportunity to work with a major company like Toyota, despite having started as an ordinary business in Coimbatore, became a major turning point for them.

He continued:

“Although we began our journey with GOAT Robotics in December 2023, we recorded a turnover of just Rs 10 lakh during 2023–2024.

“After that, we recognised our strengths, addressed our weaknesses, and began providing services to companies using various technologies in the robotics and automation sector.”

“During 2024–2025, the GOAT Robotics team began working not only with Toyota but also with several major and multinational companies, including Volvo, Maruti, Suzuki, Pricol, and Timken.

“Our turnover, which was just Rs 10 lakh, increased to Rs 6 crore in 2024–2025.

“Today, we are providing services across several countries, including India, the United States, Australia, Middle Eastern countries, Singapore, and Malaysia,” he said.

“All the members of our team come from middle-class family backgrounds and have faced considerable financial difficulties.

“Therefore, we have started an initiative to make robots accessible not only to large companies but also to small businesses.

“We are manufacturing and supplying robots at affordable prices to entrepreneurs like us,” he added.

From a 2BHK House to a Company Paying Rs 40 Lakh in Monthly Salaries

The company has robots capable of lifting or moving loads weighing 100 kg. It also manufactures robots capable of handling weights ranging from 100 kg to 5,000 kg.

To make robots accessible to ordinary entrepreneurs and micro, small, and medium enterprises, the company manufactures and sells robots priced between Rs 12–13 lakh and Rs 45 lakh, as well as robots valued between Rs 45 lakh and Rs 2 crore.

“Our journey, which began in a simple 2BHK house, has grown to the point where we established our own dedicated 6,000 sq. ft. office in 2024.

“Our company, which started with just nine people in Coimbatore, now employs 77 people.

“We provide opportunities to engineering graduates who are eager to learn and develop their knowledge after completing their education.

“We offer a minimum salary of Rs 30,000. Every month, we spend a total of Rs 40 lakh on salaries alone for the staff and interns working at GOAT Robotics,” Muthu proudly shared, describing the company's growth.

“There are nine of us. This success has been possible because each of us works in teams of two.

“We have divided ourselves into teams based on our experience in manufacturing, communication, service, marketing, and research and development. This division of responsibilities has made it easier for us to achieve success.”

“Every year, the Central Government encourages micro, small, and medium entrepreneurs by presenting awards.

“In 2025, we won the Central Government's Make in India Excellence Award 2025 and received a cash prize of Rs 10 lakh from the government.

“So far in the current financial year alone, we have achieved a turnover of Rs 8 crore.

“Our target is to reach a turnover of Rs 25 crore during this financial year,” he said.

In March 2025, the company raised Rs 2.66 crore (approximately $311K–$320K) in a funding round led by Campus Angels Network, with participation from TiE Coimbatore, NativeLead Angels, Pontaq Ventures, and others.

“Deep Affection Is What Will Make Us Successful”

Muthu also offered some advice to people planning to start a new business and those considering starting a business with partners.

“Those who run businesses with friends or other partners can achieve great success only if they always have deep affection and care for one another.

“When failures occur, they must be willing to make compromises, support one another, face problems positively, and overcome difficult times together. By doing so, they can achieve success more easily.

“Similarly, when starting something worthwhile, we should not wait for the right time. We must understand the risks involved and start the business immediately.

“If we simply watch from the sidelines or hesitate, time will leave us behind, and we may not even be able to begin what we had planned.

“If we lose time, we will neither be able to take risks nor grow,” Muthu Vangaliyappan said, sharing the lessons he had learned from his entrepreneurial journey.

item.title: Lakshmi Venu seeks formal partition of TVS Venu Srinivasan family assets
item.description: In a partition notice to her father, she has called upon him, as head of the family, to discharge his fiduciary duties and give effect to a fair and lawful partition.
item.content:encoded:
Lakshmi Venu, daughter of industrialist Venu Srinivasan, has formally sought partition of the joint family assets of a branch of the TVS family.

In a partition notice to her father, she has called upon him, as head of the family, to discharge his fiduciary duties and give effect to a fair and lawful partition.

Lakshmi, in her statement on Monday, asserted that, under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as amended in 2005, she is entitled to her rightful share in the joint family property and has an independent right to seek its partition.

Her claim is also founded on the equal rights of daughters recognised under Section 6 of the Act.

Stating that the assets for which she seeks partition include the family interests held through the VS Trust and other holding vehicles and structures, she said, "These encompass the businesses and assets allotted to the Venu Srinivasan branch under the 2020 TVS family arrangement, including interests in TVS Holdings, TVS Motor Company, TVS Credit Services and Sundaram-Clayton".

Lakshmi maintained that the larger TVS family arrangement did not constitute a partition within the Venu Srinivasan family. No settlement or partition of the assets within her immediate family was ever initiated, let alone concluded.

In her view, management does not confer exclusive ownership or extinguish lawful rights of other family members.

Lakshmi contended that she is being wrongfully denied her rightful share of the joint family property and alleged that the concentration of beneficial interest in favour of her brother was to the exclusion of her own lawful rights.

She regarded these actions not only as a breach of law but also as a breach of trust."Patriarchy has no place in law or in a progressive India. The rights of daughters to joint family property cannot be overridden through unilateral decisions or corporate arrangements", she added.

Reiterating her preference for an amicable and equitable resolution, Lakshmi has called for the matter to be settled with fairness, dignity and respect for the rights of all family members.

Meanwhile, another statement from Mallika Srinivasan, MD, Tractors and Farm Equipment Limited, supporting her daughter Lakshmi Venu's legitimate right in the family assets, said, "It is unfortunate that requests for an amicable settlement have not so far progressed in a meaningful and timely way".

She further said, "As a mother, to me, a son and daughter are equal in every respect. I do believe that Lakshmi has a legitimate share of the family assets, not unequal to that of (Lakshmi's brother) Sudarshan’s. I reiterate that this is a matter to be settled, in the interests of all stakeholders, through transparent dialogue, with equity, clarity and amity. I sincerely hope that we can move forward constructively, with grace and dignity".

item.title: Emerging cryptographic requirements and the transition to quantum-resistant security
item.description: Encryption forms the backbone of our everyday digital lives including banking transactions, healthcare and communication. However, the rise of quantum computing is challenging our assumptions about how long certain types of security will remain effective.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine a scenario where confidential information that was encrypted and sent years ago is suddenly able to be decrypted. The security systems worked as intended, the information was exchanged, the encryption algorithms were considered secure and there was no evidence of a breach. However, advances in computing have made that formerly secure information vulnerable. This is a concern that is driving the discussion about quantum resistant security.

We use encryption to secure almost every aspect of our digital lives. From banking transactions and healthcare data to industrial communications and defence systems, the encryption algorithms we use to secure sensitive information have been trusted for decades. However, the rise of quantum computing is challenging our assumptions about how long certain types of security will remain effective.

While quantum computers that can crack popular public-key cryptography aren't currently available, the possibility of this is an important consideration for organisations that need to ensure long term security of data.

Understanding the threat of quantum

Cybersecurity as we know it today relies on different types of cryptography for different purposes. We use Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) algorithms to secure data. We use public-key cryptography like RSA and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) for securing key establishment, authentication and digital signatures.

Quantum computing presents different challenges to these cryptographic systems. With Shor's algorithm, a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could potentially solve the mathematical problems behind RSA and ECC, thus compromising systems that rely on these cryptographic systems.

With Grover's algorithm, we have the theoretical speed up for searching for keys in symmetric encryption. For AES-256, this reduces the theoretical security margin against brute force attacks, however, this doesn't make AES-256 practically breakable with current quantum computing. This is important because we need to know what types of cryptographic systems are most at risk before we can determine what we need to change.

Another concern is that attackers could potentially collect encrypted information today, and hold on to it for decryption in the future. This approach is called harvest now, decrypt later, and it poses risks for information that must be secure for many years. Sensitive defence communications, financial data, intellectual property may remain valuable for a long time after the initial transmission.

Why existing infrastructure makes the transition difficult

While replacing an encryption algorithm may seem like a simple task, the digital infrastructure we use today consists of multiple interconnected systems with different security needs.

For example, imagine an industrial facility with hundreds of connected sensors, controllers and communication devices. Some of these devices may have been installed years ago, and may remain in use for another decade. Others may have limited processing power, memory or network connectivity.We need to consider carefully when introducing new cryptographic mechanisms to these systems.

With post-quantum cryptographic algorithms we may need larger keys, signatures, or more processing compared to current public-key cryptographic mechanisms. These differences can impact communication bandwidth, memory usage and processing performance. For real-time devices, any changes in computational requirements may impact the system design.

Thus, we need to consider the entire security architecture. This includes device authentication, key management, communication protocols and hardware compatibility. It's not just about updating software to make it quantum resistant.

What do emerging cryptographic standards mean?

We are starting to see the shift towards post-quantum cryptography. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) finalised three post-quantum cryptographic standards in August 2024. These are: ML-KEM for key establishment, and ML-DSA and SLH-DSA for digital signatures.

These standards provide organisations with defined cryptographic mechanisms designed to resist attacks from both conventional and quantum computers. However, implementing these standards isn't just a matter of replacing cryptographic algorithms.

We need to identify vulnerable cryptography that we use, understand how encryption keys are generated and exchanged, and consider whether existing systems can support the requirements. Alternative approaches like out-of-band key distribution, and quantum key distribution are also being explored. These approaches offer different security properties, but come with practical considerations such as infrastructure, cost, scalability and interoperability.

There's no one size fits all approach that meets all operational requirements. The right architecture depends on the sensitivity of the information, devices involved and environment where communication occurs.

Building cryptographic agility into security systems

One of the most important things organisations can do to prepare is to build cryptographic agility. This involves designing systems that can adapt to changes in cryptographic algorithms and protocols without major infrastructure changes.

●      Firstly, organisations need to understand their cryptographic dependencies. What cryptographic algorithms are being used? Where are the keys being stored? How are devices authenticated? What systems may be challenging to update?

●      Secondly, prioritise. Systems protecting sensitive long-lived information, or systems in critical infrastructure may need earlier planning for migration.

Using hybrid cryptographic approaches (using both existing classical mechanisms and post-quantum cryptographic algorithms) can help in managing the transition while still being compatible during the migration process.

For connected and embedded systems, security should also be considered when designing hardware and software. Devices that are expected to be in use for many years should support secure updates and be adaptable to changing cryptographic mechanisms where technically possible.

Preparing before the threat becomes imminent

Transitioning to quantum resistant security will be a gradual process. With existing infrastructure, operational constraints and evolving standards, organisations will need to carefully plan for migration strategies.

This is especially challenging for sectors like banking, telecommunications, manufacturing and defence, where we often have sensitive information and connected infrastructure with long operational lifecycles.

We don't need quantum computing to be an imminent threat to start preparing. Information encrypted today may need to be secure for decades. Systems deployed today may be in use long after the cryptographic requirements have changed.

The focus should be on understanding our current vulnerabilities, considering emerging standards and building systems that can adapt to the changing landscape of cryptographic technology.

The future of cybersecurity will be as much about being able to update and maintain trusted security as it is about the strength of the encryption algorithms we use.

~ By Srinivas Shekar, Co-Founder and CEO, Pantherun Technologies

item.title: Karnataka aims to become global hub for frontier technologies: DK Shivakumar
item.description: Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar said the strong technology ecosystem in the State gives it the advantage to lead in areas such as AI, biotech, semiconductor and robotics.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), deeptech, semiconductor, robotics, and biotech, said Chief Minister DK Shivakumar at the inaugural of Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) in Bengaluru on Tuesday, citing the state government's enabling policies.

BTS, now in its 29th edition, is themed “AI and Beyond”. Addressing the event, the Chief Minister highlighted that Karnataka has consistently been at the forefront of technology and is well positioned to lead the next phase of global innovation backed by strong IT and startup ecosystem.

The Chief Minister said Karnataka accounted for two out of every five dollars earned by India through software and services exports, which amounted to approximately $173 billion last year.

The state also attracted $9.4 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI) equity inflows in the first half of FY26, accounting for 26.7% of India's total inflows during the period. Bengaluru is home to more than 1,000 Global Capability Centres (GCCs), while over 30 new GCCs brought investments of more than $1 billion into Karnataka in 2025.

Shivakumar said Karnataka was home to more than 24,000 recognised startups, with nearly two out of every five Indian unicorns (startups valued at $1 billion or more) originating from the state.

Bengaluru ranked eighth among the world's startup ecosystems and second in Asia for AI-native startups. Startups in Karnataka have collectively raised approximately $79 billion, while women founders in Bengaluru have secured $13.4 billion in funding.

The state government is also extending financial support to startups working on emerging technologies. Through its ELEVATE initiative, it has supported nearly 1,500 startups with equity-free grants worth $41 million over the past decade.

Under ELEVATE NxT, deeptech startups are eligible for grants of up to Rs 1 crore. Since last year, 33 startups have received equity-free funding totalling Rs 30 crore.

The government has also announced Innoverse, a deeptech accelerator that will support 35 growth-stage ventures over the next five years. The programme aims to help startups move beyond product development and scale up to industrial-level operations.

Another initiative, Government First, aims to make the state government an early customer for startups. A dedicated fund of Rs 25 crore has been earmarked to procure innovative solutions developed by these companies.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is another main focus of Karnataka's technology ambitions. Shivakumar said Bengaluru accounted for nearly 50% of India's AI and machine learning talent.

The state is also building what he described as India's first government-led AI university, alongside an AI Hub that will bring startups, researchers and industry stakeholders together.

An additional Centre of Excellence at IIIT Raichur will focus on expanding AI applications across 13 districts of North Karnataka, particularly in sectors such as agriculture, healthcare, education and small businesses.

Karnataka is also looking to strengthen its position in the semiconductor industry. The state is home to more than 100 fabless chip companies, while Bengaluru accounts for three out of every five engineers working in India's semiconductor capability centres, Shivakumar said.

The state currently accounts for one-fifth of India's electronics exports. Its next priority is to expand beyond chip design and build manufacturing capabilities.

item.title: Elastic{ON} Mumbai: Why context, not the model, is the real AI advantage
item.description: At Elastic{ON} Mumbai, CEO Ash Kulkarni argued that every business already owns what AI models lack. The rest of the day showed what it takes to put that context to work.
item.content:encoded:
As AI models become available to everyone, the advantage for enterprises is shifting to something no model providers can supply: the context that makes AI useful to a specific business. Elastic{ON} Mumbai took on that challenge, bringing together the people building and running AI in India’s enterprises to work out how to make their data count.

The Elastic{ON} Tour 2026/2027 stopped in Mumbai on September 30, bringing developers, SREs, IT and security leaders and practitioners to JW Marriott Mumbai Sahar under the theme ‘Forge the Future’. Across keynotes, live demos, customer and partner sessions, and a hackathon awards ceremony, one idea kept returning: context is what turns a widely available model into a lasting business advantage.

Context is your moat

Ash Kulkarni, CEO of Elastic, who grew up a short distance away in Vile Parle, opened by tying the company’s name to the city. “Mumbai has stretched, it has evolved, it has transformed. It has never broken,” he said.

That adaptability matters, he argued, because AI is moving faster than any earlier technology shift, and the models driving it share a blind spot. “None of these models have any understanding of your business. They don’t understand your data,” Kulkarni said. “The bottleneck is the context.”

Every industry now faces startups trading human capital for token capital. What they cannot copy, Kulkarni said, is a company’s accumulated learnings, experience, and data on how best to serve its customers and partners. “That context is your moat.”

The challenge is that context is scattered. Customer information alone sits across CRM, entitlement, and ticketing systems. Kulkarni’s answer is a bridge that connects it all, securely and with privacy built in, to any model. The result, he said, is “actual intelligence”: the reasoning power of the model combined with the context of the business. Delivering that has meant evolving Elastic’s core engine.

Making context affordable

Ajay Nair, GM, Elasticsearch and Platform, Elastic, picked up the thread. “The model’s only half the equation,” he said. An agent that does not know a customer has raised ten support tickets might still send them a renewal pitch, and that will not go well.

Nair said most teams make their models rebuild context from scratch every time a question is asked, an approach he called “top-down” context that burns tokens on every query. The more efficient pattern is “bottom-up”: deriving relationships, metadata, and risk factors once, keeping them fresh, and handing models a ready-made picture.

That is the idea behind the Elastic Context Engine, which Nair announced on stage and which is now in private preview.

Context at work in operations and security

The same foundation runs through Elastic’s observability and security solutions. Vinay Chandrasekhar, Director of Product Management, Observability, Elastic, demonstrated Elastic nightshift AI SRE, an AI agent that surfaces problems no alert was set up to catch, tests several root-cause hypotheses in parallel, and shows every step of its reasoning. Kulkarni noted that it gets better at investigating “within the context of your environment”, adding: “It’s not generic.” Elastic has since announced nightshift in private preview on Elastic Observability Serverless.

James Spiteri, Senior Director of Product Management, Elastic, argued that “the SIEM has never mattered more”. He previewed what has since launched as AlertZero, the agentic layer built into Elastic Security. Specialised groups of agents, called Watches, triage alerts, hunt for threats, and investigate incidents, learning from how a team already works, while analysts decide which actions need their approval. AlertZero is now available in technical preview across Elastic Cloud, self-managed, and air-gapped environments.

A day built with the community

Beyond the keynotes, customers carried much of the program. On the morning panel, moderated by Ravindra Ramnani, Head of Field Engineering at Elastic India, leaders from Axis Bank, Standard Chartered Bank, and Easebuzz debated whether enterprises can observe, audit, and explain what their AI agents do. Nykaa joined AWS to describe how its SREs now investigate incidents by querying logs conversationally with Elastic AI Assistant. Afternoon breakouts featured Network18 on AI governance, Qualys on closing the SOC loop with agentic AI, and Standard Chartered Bank on standardising observability across 40 countries, alongside community sessions from Iron Mountain, Jolera, and Sprinklr.

Partners showed how they ground AI in enterprise context. Google Cloud explained how its agent tooling and Gemini models work with Elastic retrieval to turn sensitive enterprise data into trusted context without moving it. Microsoft and Elastic walked through OverflowAI, Stack Overflow’s retrieval-first architecture, in which Elasticsearch hybrid retrieval grounds Azure OpenAI in the community’s validated answers.

The community also had its moment on the main stage, as the Forge the Future Hackathon awards recognised the top teams from the Grand Finale held in Bengaluru on September 18 and 19. Frustrated Engineers took first place, followed by Sandboxed in second and Defcon in third. Powered by Elastic and AWS, the hackathon challenged teams to build explainable, production-ready AI agents across search, observability, and security.

Models will change. Context stays.

Kulkarni closed with commitments that put a customer’s context, not any single model, at the centre. Elastic will stay model agnostic, he said, because “there is no winner yet, and there will likely never be a single winner.” It will also run wherever customers do, in the cloud or self-managed.

Models will keep getting better. The context that makes them useful belongs to the business, and Elastic{ON} Mumbai made the case that connecting the two is where the lasting advantage lies.

item.title: How AI could reshape jobs, investing, and wealth creation in India
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Angel One Group CEO Ambarish Kenghe discussed how AI could change the nature of work, make investing more accessible, and create opportunities in healthcare, transportation, fintech and beyond.
item.content:encoded:
AI is changing how people work, how businesses build products, and how investors identify opportunities. As the technology becomes more accessible, the question is how more Indians can participate in the wealth it creates.

At TechSparks 2026, Ambarish Kenghe, Group CEO of Angel One, joined Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, for a fireside chat on investing in India’s AI decade. The conversation covered the future of jobs, AI’s role in making investing more accessible, and the sectors where new opportunities could emerge.

Will AI create more jobs than it replaces?

For Kenghe, the answer lies partly in how technology has changed economies in the past.

He pointed to Jevons paradox, named after British economist William Stanley Jevons, who observed that improvements in steam engine efficiency led to an increase in coal consumption rather than a decline. As engines became more efficient, their use expanded.

Kenghe believes AI could have a similar effect. Citing data from Anthropic, he noted that 57% of the work done with Claude involves augmentation, while 43% involves automation. As AI makes knowledge work more productive, demand for such work could increase in ways that are difficult to predict.

He cited banking as an example. When ATMs and computerized systems began replacing manual transactions at bank counters, it seemed likely that fewer employees would be needed. Instead, banking jobs increased as the industry expanded and new requirements emerged.

Kenghe believes AI could have a similar impact, allowing people to work on problems that have remained unresolved.

However, the transition will require workers to adapt.

“While the demand for knowledge work will go up a lot with AI, each of us will have to transform because it’s not that we will do the same kind of job. We can’t become more efficient tellers. We will have to get to a very different level of operation, and what we do will change. How it will change, only time will tell,” he said.

Making investing more accessible

The conversation then turned to how more Indians could participate in wealth creation.

Kenghe identified three challenges: access, information, and intelligence.

Access to investing has become considerably easier. People can now complete their KYC on their phones and start investing without the physical paperwork and complicated procedures that were once required.

However, access alone does not guarantee participation. Many people know about the stock market but lack the information or confidence to make investment decisions.

“The two other issues which are not fully solved are information and intelligence, and I think AI is solving it in a big way,” Kenghe said.

He cited Angel One’s Ask Angel, an AI-powered tool that allows users to ask questions and receive relevant information. The tool does not provide investment advice because of regulatory restrictions.

Kenghe also believes AI could help reduce some of the advantages institutional investors have over individual investors. Institutions typically have access to more capital, sophisticated technology, and specialized teams. While AI cannot eliminate these differences, it could make information and tools more widely available.

He compared this development to the evolution of computing. The computer used aboard the Apollo mission had far less computing power than modern devices. Today, smartphones offer computing capabilities that far exceed what was available during that mission.

He believes investing could undergo a similar change as AI tools become more accessible.

Citing a SEBI study, Kenghe said 63% of Indian households are aware of the stock market, but only 9.5% invest in it. Better access to information and intelligence could encourage more people to participate.

However, broader participation will not necessarily lead to equal wealth creation. AI could democratize access to investing without socialising wealth. Individual investors would still need to make decisions based on their available capital and appetite for risk.

Building products that solve real problems

Drawing on his experience building Google Pay, Kenghe discussed what it takes to create products that consumers want to use.

For him, the starting point is identifying a genuine problem and solving it well.

A product may be complex behind the scenes, but the experience should be simple for the user. In payments, for example, people want to transfer money quickly and reliably while knowing their transactions are secure.

Adding features serves little purpose if the basic experience does not work.

Kenghe said identifying the right problem is often the harder task. Founders can become distracted by new technologies and trends, but product development should begin with understanding what users need.

Where the next opportunities lie

When Sharma asked about untapped areas for innovation, Kenghe pointed to opportunities beyond building increasingly large AI models.

He cited Jev AI, a model focused on efficiency rather than competing directly on size, as an example of an alternative approach to AI development. He also mentioned Instinct as another example of companies approaching the technology differently.

Healthcare, he believes, offers considerable scope for specialized AI models.

“I don't see anybody coming out with a kick-ass, dedicated healthcare model. You could actually create models that are dedicated to certain diseases, certain areas,” he said.

Rather than approaching healthcare as a single, broad problem, Kenghe suggested developing models focused on specific diseases or areas of care.

He also identified transportation and logistics as sectors with significant opportunities. While self-driving technology is beginning to develop, he believes there is still considerable room for innovation, particularly in India, where traffic and logistics costs remain major challenges.

Other areas he is optimistic about include space exploration, with the long-term possibility of space-based data centres, and fintech.

Balancing ambition with data

For entrepreneurs, identifying an opportunity is only the beginning. They must also make decisions amid uncertainty.

Kenghe believes data should inform these decisions without determining every move.

It can help founders understand market conditions, assess risks, and make more rational choices. But data cannot provide every answer, particularly when entrepreneurs are building something new.

“Entrepreneurs are entrepreneurs because their emotion brings in the passion. Take the emotion out of it, perhaps the passion comes out as well,” he said.

Kenghe believes founders need to balance that passion with evidence. Regularly reviewing data can help them make informed decisions and remain grounded, while recognizing its limitations leaves room for instinct, conviction, and the risks involved in building a business.

item.title: Redbrick Offices raises Rs 630 Cr in equity led by India SME Investments and Abakkus
item.description: Redbrick said it plans to use the capital to expand its managed offices portfolio from about 6.5 million sq. ft. to more than 10 million sq. ft. over the next 18 to 24 months, while investing in technology, design and service delivery to cater to enterprise and GCC clients.
item.content:encoded:
Redbrick Offices has raised about $72 million (Rs 630 crore) in equity across its Series A and A1 funding rounds, the company said. The funding comprises a large primary infusion and a smaller secondary component.

India SME Investments led the Series A round in March 2026, while the Series A1 round was recently led by Abakkus’s Four2Eight Opportunities Fund. Evolvence Equity Partners, IIFL Capital Asset Management and UTI Alternatives, among others, also participated in the extended round. India SME Investments made a follow-on investment as part of Series A1. UTI Alternatives had earlier invested in the company through a structured convertible debenture issuance in March 2025.

Redbrick said it plans to use the capital to expand its managed offices portfolio from about 6.5 million sq. ft. to more than 10 million sq. ft. over the next 18 to 24 months. It will also use the funds to serve workspace requirements of large enterprises and global capability centres (GCCs), and to invest in technology infrastructure, design, and service delivery. The company said it is open to strategic partnerships and acquisitions that fit its growth plans.

The fundraise comes as India’s flexible office market crosses 100 million sq. ft., driven by demand from large enterprises and GCCs, according to the company.

“This investment marks an important milestone in our journey,” said Ayush Goenka, chairman and managing director of Redbrick Offices. He said the backing from India SME, Abakkus and other investors validates the company’s focus on improving unit economics and on demand-backed, profitable growth.

Ankit Aggarwal, senior vice president and senior fund manager for private equity at Abakkus, called Redbrick a capital-efficient business that has scaled while remaining profitable. He said flexible, asset-light corporate spaces are becoming a core part of real estate strategy for multinationals and GCCs in India.

Mitin Jain, founder and managing partner of India SME Investments, said the firm’s March 2026 decision to back Redbrick was based on its belief in Goenka and the management team’s record of building a sizeable, bootstrapped business with a focus on profitable growth.

Ladderup Corporate Advisory and IIFL Capital Services were financial advisers to the company, and Rajani Associates was its legal adviser.

Redbrick Offices operates about 6.5 million sq. ft. across more than 70 centres in over eight Indian cities, with more than 1.15 lakh seats. It builds Grade-A offices to client specifications and provides facilities management and hospitality-led services through its wholly owned subsidiary, Snow White Technologies & Services Private Limited. Its clients include GCCs, Fortune 500 companies, large enterprises, BFSI firms and US-based multinationals.

item.title: Former Freshworks executives-founded AI startup Dreamteam raises $53M
item.description: Dreamteam raised this funding from Together Fund, Accel and Premji Invest and this capital will be primarily used to enhance its tech platform
item.content:encoded:
Dreamteam, an AI native customer relationship management (CRM) startup founded by former executives of Freshworks, has raised $53 million in funding from Together Fund, Accel and Premji Invest.

Founded in 2025 by Anand Venkatraman, Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy with headquarters in California and core engineering team in Chennai, is building a technology platform that can understand customer context and have the right AI coworkers to execute.

“The CRM was supposed to give companies a complete picture of their customers, yet the richest parts of that picture have always lived outside the CRM,” said Anand Venkatraman, Co-founder and CEO of Dreamteam.

“AI finally gives us a way to change that foundation. Dreamteam learns from the work your team is already doing, keeps the context alive and gives every salesperson skilled AI teammates that can reason over it and move deals forward. Your sellers and leaders can spend their time on relationships, judgement and closing deals, while Dreamteam takes care of everything required around them,” he said.

According to a statement from Dreamteam, companies across diverse industries, including AI, online media, healthcare, manufacturing, and consulting are using their technology platform.

Girish Mathrubootham, Founding partner at Together Fund, the first institutional investor in Dreamteam added: “CRM is among the biggest software categories ripe for disruption. I've worked alongside Dreamteam's founders since day one as their vision for an AI-native CRM took shape. Their deep CRM expertise and proven record of scaling enterprise software make them uniquely positioned to lead this reinvention.”

Looking ahead, Dreamteam aims to extend its intelligence layer beyond sales to the entire customer lifecycle, including prospecting, onboarding, customer success and upselling. The company also offers Magic Apps, which allows business users to create custom applications and dashboards using natural language without writing code.

Shekhar Kirani, Partner at Accel said, “In the AI era, the companies that understand their customers deeply have an enormous advantage. Today, everyone on a team sees a different version of the customer, because no central system holds all the information. Dreamteam is building that system with AI agents.”

item.title: India has 300,000 startups; farmers open to using technologies, says Union minister Jayant Chaudhary
item.description: The conference was held alongside the Singapore-India Hackathon at the Singapore Management University (SMU) here.
item.content:encoded:
India has around 300,000 registered startups, many of which are led by women, Union minister Jayant Chaudhary told global tech leaders on Tuesday, and underlined that farmers across the country are also enthusiastic about using technology.

"Farmers are not going to be developers of any tech solutions for the future, but they are users (and) they are very open to using technologies," he told over 300 delegates at the TIECON 2026 conference organised by The Indus Entrepreneurs (TiEcon) in Singapore.

"With the farmers, there is great enthusiasm," the minister of state for skill development and entrepreneurship said.

The conference was held alongside the Singapore-India Hackathon at the Singapore Management University (SMU) here.

Highlighting the success of startups in India, the minister said that the country has nearly 300,000 registered startups today, which are from Tier-II and Tier-III cities. A lot of these startups are led by women.

"Our seeds are sown throughout the country," he said, adding that it is not just Bengaluru, Mumbai or Hyderabad -- the traditional power centres where the startups have grown and established a global footprint.

"So, that is the great potential," Chaudhury said as he described the Indian startup ecosystem. "India's startup story today is very, very robust."

"A great depth is in the fact that our academia is also contributing today to the research. Our universities are no longer closed. They are contributing to research innovation. Our professors are part of some of these boards (of the startups)," said the minister.

He further shared that the Indian Institutes of Technologies are now launching deep tech funds. "They (the IITs) are working with some of the fund management companies, and trying to get even small ticket investors to come (to India) and work for the future."

"So, that gives me great confidence that the Indian story is (scaling) with such a young population," he underlined.

TiE Singapore President Prantik Mazumdar welcomed Minister Chaudhary's update on the startup ecosystem in India.

"We are grateful to Shri Jayant Chaudhary for his presence and support of our ambitions, and share his belief in the importance of investing in human capital.

"With TiEcon SG 2026, we want to explore how we can harness the complementary strengths of Singapore and India to build the next generation of global technology giants from Asia. By deepening our collaboration with institutions such as Singapore Management University, we hope to nurture entrepreneurial talent and facilitate greater talent mobility between the two countries," said Mazumdar.

Themed 'Frontier Tech Reshaping The Coming Decade', the one-day conference brought together a distinguished community of founders, investors, policymakers, business leaders, and technology and innovation leaders to explore trends, technologies, and opportunities shaping the next decade of venture building.

The TIECON SG 2026 conference celebrated 25 years of TiE in Singapore.

item.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 17, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Tuesday, November 17, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
From Pragya's Misra's new role at OpenAI to CarDekho Group appointing new CEO to PhonePe partnering with Kerala Startup Mission, YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond.

Latest

Pragya Misra to lead OpenAI's biz development in India and South Asia

Pragya Misra, OpenAI's head of strategy and global affairs in India, will be taking up a new role where she will be leading the firm's business development for India and South Asia region. 

Announcing the news on Linkedin, she said, "In this new role, I'll focus on building partnerships that help businesses transform with AI, bring our technology to millions more people, and build the infrastructure needed to support this growth," she said.

Misra was OpenAI's first hire in India, in 2024. Prior to joining OpenAI, she worked with Truecaller and Meta.

CarDekho Group appoints Sudhir Pai as CEO

CarDekho Group has appointed Sudhir Pai as CEO– Auto Classifieds and Group Strategy Head. He will lead the Group's core auto classifieds business, including CarDekho.com, ZigWheels and BikeDekho, etc while also driving strategic initiatives and long-term growth priorities across the Group.

Sudhir joins CarDekho Group after nearly 15 years as Chief Executive Officer of Magicbricks, the Times Internet-owned property platform, which he led from 2011 to early 2026.

He brings over two decades of leadership experience across the internet, FMCG, medical electronics and banking. Before Magicbricks, he held roles at Marico, Hindustan Unilever, Citibank and Wipro GE Medical Systems. He holds an MBA from the Symbiosis Centre for Management & HRD, Pune, and a Bachelor of Engineering from Goa University.

PhonePe partners with Kerala Startup Mission

PhonePe announced a strategic partnership with Kerala Startup Mission (KSUM) to accelerate the growth of the state’s entrepreneurial ecosystem.

This collaboration will focus on three factors: Seamless Payment Infrastructure: Through PhonePe Payment Gateway, these startups will be able to seamlessly integrate reliable, high-success rate digital payment solutions. Secondly, PhonePe will provide KSUM-registered startups with dedicated onboarding assistance and priority technical support and PhonePe & KSUM will jointly drive ecosystem-building initiatives by hosting specialized workshops and knowledge-sharing sessions.

Accenture LearnVantage and Google Cloud to bring AI Learning to more than 1,000 schools and colleges

Accenture LearnVantage and Google Cloud announced a strategic collaboration to bring industry-aligned AI learning to students and educators across more than 1,000 schools and colleges in India. 

The initiative aims to provide hands-on tools and certifications designed to prepare students for an AI-driven economy.

 

Accenture LearnVantage and Google Cloud will focus on enabling more than 1,000 public and private schools and colleges in India to accelerate digital and AI transformation. These learning programs are designed to deliver scalable, AI-powered learning experiences that are immersive, relevant and aligned to industry needs. 

The companies will launch the program at higher education institutions and school networks.

Funding

AI video company Lemonpeel raises $1M

Lemonpeel, an AI video production company for enterprise creative teams, has raised about $1 million in a pre-seed funding round led by Shastra VC, with participation from Rukam Sitara and angel investors. The company will use the capital to develop its multi-agent platform for video creation, editing, quality checks and delivery.

It will also invest in marketing and go-to-market capabilities to reach more enterprise creative teams, and build intellectual property around faces and creative workflows.

Founded in September 2025 by Hardik Goyal, Riddhiman Pal and Abhinav Nikam, Mumbai- headquartered Lemonpeel works with customers in India and the UAE, including 5 of NIFTY 50 companies and notable global E-comm players.

Personal finance startup Finny.club raises angel funding

Finny.club, an AI-first personal CFO fast-tracking financial independence (FIRE) for salaried families, has raised Rs 5.3 Cr (~$560K) in an angel funding round.

The round saw participation from Ramanathan RV, founder of Hyperface and Juspay; Anil Goel, Global CTO, Nielsen; Uday Sodhi (ex-Sony Pictures); Aditya Pittie, MD & CEO, Pittie Group; and Zorvian LLP, an angel syndicate, among other angel investors.

Founded in 2024 by Rohit Tuteja (ex-HealthifyMe, upGrad, OYO) and Sachin Kamkar (ex-Myntra, Tracxn, Hyperface), finny.club helps salaried Indians plan their retirement and become financially independent.

The fresh capital will be deployed across three key areas: R&D with a focus on AI-led product development, growing the financial advisory team and marketing.

Karta AI raises Rs 28.52 crore in seed funding

Karta AI (Dreamzest Technologies Private Limited) raised Rs 28.52 crore seed funding round led by Peer Capital and Cedar Hill Capital. 

The round also saw participation from Wyser VC, CDM Capital and Seedstars.

The fresh capital will be used largely to expand distribution and strengthen the team, with a focus on its predictive context engine and automating more complex customer workflows reliably.

Other news

Ranveer Singh and Aman Gupta launches H.I.M

Ranveer Singh and Aman Gupta launched H.I.M (Handsome Indian Man), a men's personal care brand formulated specifically for Indian skin, the Indian climate and Indian biology. 


H.I.M debuts with eight products across face, body and hair, each powered by IN·XT™, a proprietary molecule developed exclusively for the brand. 


The H.I.M range is priced from Rs299 to Rs 899 and is available from today on HIM Science Website, Amazon and Blinkit.

Technology and investment solutions provider SEI opens GCC in Hyderabad

SEI, a global provider of financial technology, operations and asset management services, today opened its Global Capability Centre (GCC) in Hyderabad. 

Headquartered in Oaks, Pennsylvania, USA, SEI currently supports a team of 800 professionals in Hyderabad and is rapidly scaling its operations. 

Located in Hi-Tech City, its nearly 137,000 sq. ft. facility with capacity for 1,200 workstations serves as a strategic hub bringing together technology and operations.

Electric mobility platform Bijliride is partnering with MOWO social initiatives

Electric mobility platform Bijliride is partnering with MOWO Social Initiatives to accelerate women’s participation in the commercial mobility workforce. In a strategic collaboration with the Telangana Police, the initiative provides women in Hyderabad with comprehensive driver training.

Designed to bridge the gender gap in the mobility sector, the programme requires no prior driving experience. It offers an end-to-end support system, encompassing free electric scooter and auto-rickshaw driving training, road safety education, and guidance on obtaining a driving license. 

The initiative also provides job-placement support, vehicle-rental assistance, and three months of dedicated mentorship and counseling to help participants build confidence and safely navigate their new careers.

MapmyIndia Mappls app integrates with Arattai

MapmyIndia Mappls announced the integration of its flagship Mappls App with Arattai, an instant messaging and VoIP calling app from global technology company Zoho Corporation. 

With this integration, locations shared in Arattai chats and groups can now be opened directly in the Mappls App, allowing users to get directions and navigate to their destination without copying addresses or switching between multiple apps.

The users can open a chat or group on Arattai, tap on the shared location, select ‘Get directions’ and select Mappls Maps. The Mappls App displays the route to the shared location along with the estimated travel time, distance and trip cost.

item.title: Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier tech; Fadnavis’ vision for a new Maharashtra
item.description: Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier technologies such as AI, deeptech, and biotech, said CM DK Shivakumar at Bengaluru Tech Summit. Meanwhile, Maharashtra CM Fadnavis has shared his roadmap for a trillion-dollar, drought-free, deeptech Maharashtra by 2035.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

The best of AI is yet to come. 

The potential of artificial intelligence still remains unexplored, and it can help create solutions with population-scale impact, said panellists during a discussion at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026. 

Karnataka Home and IT Minister Priyank Kharge, Infosys Co-founder S Gopalakrishnan, Biocon Group Chairperson Kiran Mazumdar Shaw, and Accel India Founding Partner Prashanth Prakash stressed the opportunities in areas such as drug development, cybersecurity, IT solutions, governance and services. 

At another conference across the world, Union Minister Jayant Chaudhary spoke about India’s robust startup story. 

India has around 300,000 registered startups, many of which are led by women, the Minister of State for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship told global tech leaders at the TIECON 2026 conference in Singapore. “Our seeds are sown throughout the country,” he said. Highlighting the market potential, he pointed out that Indian farmers are keen to use technology, and the IITs are launching deeptech funds. 

Moving on, ecommerce giant Amazon plans to invest an additional $7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, as it seeks to meet growing electricity requirements and reduce the carbon intensity of power across its operations.

In other news, Pragya Misra, OpenAI’s head of strategy and global affairs in India, is taking on a new role. She will lead the firm’s business development for India and South Asia, with a focus on building partnerships that help businesses transform with AI. 

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • Karnataka’s aim to become a global hub for frontier tech
  • Fadnavis’ vision for a new Maharashtra

Here’s your trivia for today: What cloud-based gaming service did Google launch in 2019, only to shut it down in 2023 due to lack of adoption? (Scroll down for the answer)

Technology

Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier tech

Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence, deeptech, semiconductor, robotics, and biotech, said Chief Minister DK Shivakumar at the inaugural of Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) in Bengaluru on Tuesday, citing the state government’s enabling policies.

BTS, now in its 29th edition, is themed around ‘AI and Beyond’. Addressing the event, the chief minister highlighted that Karnataka has consistently been at the forefront of technology and is well placed to lead the next phase of global innovation, backed by a strong IT and startup ecosystem.

Key takeaways 

  • Karnataka, the CM said, accounted for two out of every five dollars earned by India through software and services exports, which amounted to around $173 billion last year.
  • The state attracted $9.4 billion in FDI equity inflows in the first half of FY26, accounting for 26.7% of India’s total inflows during the period. Karnataka is home to more than 24,000 recognised startups, and nearly two out of every five Indian unicorns originate from the state, Shivakumar said. 
  • AI is another main focus of Karnataka’s technology ambitions, with Bengaluru accounting for nearly 50% of India’s AI and machine learning talent.

Roadmap

Fadnavis’ vision for a new Maharashtra

Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis spent nearly five hours judging student presentations at the summit of The Governance Challenge 2026 in Mumbai. Six finalist teams pitched their answers to one question: what can the Government of Maharashtra do to make the state an innovation hub by 2035? The teams presented ideas on healthcare, education, farming and access to credit. 

Thereafter, the chief minister, the finalists of the challenge, and Gaurav Goel, Founder & CEO of Samagra, which runs the challenge, joined Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, The Bharat Project and YourStory Media, for an open conversation.

Key takeaways: 

  • Fadnavis shared his roadmap for a trillion-dollar, drought-free, deeptech Maharashtra by 2035. The CM called Gen Z the first generation born entirely into technology, constantly connected to global best practices. Properly channelled, he said, this exposure produces bright ideas. But he stressed the need for balancing new ideas with mentoring, oversight and experience. “Innovation is a simple solution for a very complex problem,” he stressed. 
  • Goel explained that The Governance Challenge (TGC) was created to fill the gap in management education. Business school case studies, campus events, internships and placements all lean heavily towards the corporate and startup world, leaving students with little exposure to governance or social impact. TGC tries to change that through immersion, in the hope that the experience stays with students and later draws them towards nation building.
  • Shradha Sharma called the day a glimpse of what a Viksit Bharat could look like: a chief minister who listens, and young people ready to do the work.

News & updates

  • Social media curbs: Meta Platforms has fine-tuned Instagram's content recommendation systems in India to curb the visibility of sexually suggestive material and violent content, deploying more advanced AI models to identify and filter unwanted posts before they reach users.
  • Funding: Redbrick Offices, which provides managed office spaces and workspace solutions, has raised about $72 million in equity across its Series A and A1 funding rounds. The company plans to use the capital to expand its managed offices portfolio and invest in technology, design and service delivery to cater to enterprise and GCC clients.
  • Data centre curbs: The Trump administration plans to press ahead with efforts to block imports ‌of Chinese data centre equipment despite pushback from Amazon, Google, Meta and other US technology companies, according to people briefed on the matter, Reuters reported. 

What cloud-based gaming service did Google launch in 2019, only to shut it down in 2023 due to lack of adoption?

Answer: Google Stadia
