item.title: The best of AI is yet to come, say experts at Bengaluru Tech Summit
item.description: During a panel discussion, Karnataka Home and IT Minister Priyank Kharge, Infosys Co-founder S Gopalakrishnan, Biocon Group Chairperson Kiran Mazumdar Shaw, and Accel India Founding Partner Prashanth Prakash stressed the potential of AI to create solutions with population-scale impact.
item.content:encoded:
The potential of artificial intelligence (AI) still remains unexplored, and there is much more to come from this technology, in the form of solutions that will have a population scale impact, said panellists during a discussion at Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026.

During a panel discussion on the topic 'AI & Beyond: Emerging India', Karnataka Home and IT Minister Priyank Kharge highlighted how the state government is integrating AI in various departments, be it for cybersecurity or building solutions with participation from startups to improve governance.

“We ensure that we have the first mover advantage when it comes to using technology across all our departments,” the minister said.

AI has had a significant impact on the software sector and the IT industry at large, especially with the automation of the coding processes.

Infosys Co-founder S Gopalakrishnan said AI has given the opportunity to create newer kinds of products and services. While IT outsourcing will continue in its present form, AI is giving the opportunity to reimagine the entire technology stack, he said.

The technology has made deep inroads into several areas, giving rise to newer opportunities. It is also solving many unresolved problems in areas such as mathematics and biology.

Biocon Group Chairperson Kiran Mazumdar Shaw said AI is really about accelerating intelligence, and the technology will help simplify even a complex subject like biology, leading to many discoveries in medicines, diseases and diagnostics. She remarked that AI can help connect the dots to develop the next generation of drugs.

“Biology is the most important frontier for AI to be deployed. Because if you know how to deploy AI to unravel the mysteries of biology, you can unravel so many other things,” Shaw said, adding, “The real opportunity from AI is taking molecules faster from lab to clinic to patients."

Accel India Founding Partner Prashanth Prakash said the bigger opportunity in AI is not in making what is existing more efficient and more usable, but it lies in the ability to serve hundreds of millions of people by making services more affordable.

However, the biggest challenge with AI in India is availability and use of data.

Kharge felt this is an opportunity to understand the value of this technology and build solutions that are scalable and applicable for a wider section of the population.

Prakash said delivering value through AI to the rural population will be the last frontier as it still remains an unsolved sector. “It is a multi-dimensional problem as it is about the right technology from where to go, what to do, and how to grow.”

The panellists were of the view that as AI delivers value, especially through automation, one must also review the whole process and ensure a governance structure for this technology.

item.title: Malware attack hits Zoom, Salesforce and IKEA-linked websites
item.description: A malware attack reportedly used Optimizely scripts on 178 organisation websites, including Zoom, Salesforce and IKEA, to target card details and crypto wallet addresses.
item.content:encoded:
You may trust the website you are visiting. But what about the tools running behind it?

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a malware campaign involving websites linked to 178 organisations worldwide, including Zoom, Salesforce, IKEA, HSBC and Crocs. The attack shows how a compromised third-party tool can turn familiar websites into potential entry points for cybercriminals.

According to findings, the malicious code was injected through Optimizely Web, a platform companies use to run website experiments and A/B testing. This technique allows brands to show different versions of a webpage and measure how users respond.

The attack exploited that routine website function to deliver code capable of interfering with what users entered or copied on affected pages.

How a trusted website tool became a malware route

The attacker reportedly exploited a feature in Optimizely that allows customers to add JavaScript to projects. JavaScript is commonly used to make websites interactive and run features within a browser.

Malicious JavaScript was added to customer projects and delivered through Optimizely's trusted domain. This made the activity harder to identify as suspicious because the code came from a service already used by the affected websites.

Researchers at Report URI examined 1,611 Optimizely snippets and found 188 infected snippets linked to 178 organisations. The malware scanned webpages, form fields, links, images and clipboards for cryptocurrency wallet addresses.

When it detected a valid address, it could replace it with one controlled by the attacker.

A user copying a wallet address while an affected browser tab was open could therefore paste the wrong address without noticing. The malware could also capture card details entered directly into forms on affected websites.

Zoom, HSBC, IKEA and BBC among the names listed

The affected organisations spanned technology, finance, retail, travel, media and non-profit sectors.

Zoom, Salesforce and Bitly were among the technology companies named. The financial services list included HSBC US, HSBC Hong Kong and Equifax.

Retail and consumer brands such as IKEA, ASOS, Mattel, American Eagle, Crocs India and Levi's websites in several countries were also listed. Airlines including Air France-KLM and Alaska Airlines appeared in the findings, alongside media organisations such as BBC, CNN and Fox News.

Optimizely says it has fixed the issue

Optimizely said an unauthorised party exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into some customer projects.

The company said it blocked the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, removed the injected code, ended active sessions, revoked tokens and reset access for affected accounts.

The incident also exposes a security challenge for businesses that rely on third-party website tools. A website may be operated by a well-known brand, but its security also depends on the services and code it loads.

Users should keep their browsers updated, verify cryptocurrency wallet addresses before transferring funds, avoid entering payment details on suspicious pages and monitor cards for unusual transactions. A familiar brand name alone does not guarantee that every element running on its website is safe.

item.title: Credit-led fintech startup Olyv raises $6M
item.description: Founded in 2016 by Rohit Garg, Amit Chandel, Vinay Singh, and Jayant Upadhyay, Olyv offers products across personal loans, gold savings, and credit health management.
item.content:encoded:
Credit-led fintech platform Olyv has raised $6 million (~Rs57 crore) from Nippon Life India AIF Management Limited (Nippon India Alternative Investments) along with existing investors, extending the total Series B funding round to ~$30 million. 

With this investment, Nippon India Alternative Investments joins Olyv’s existing investors including Fundamentum and SMBC Asia Rising Fund. 

Founded in 2016 by Rohit Garg, Amit Chandel, Vinay Singh, and Jayant Upadhyay, Olyv offers products across personal loans, gold savings, and credit health management. 

The company said in a statement that it has nearly 2 million monthly active users and more than 5 crore app downloads, and serves customers across 19,000+ pin codes in India.

Olyv also said it has disbursed ~80 lakh loans and facilitated ~Rs13,000 crore in cumulative transactions, while consistently increasing PAT profitability for 14 consecutive quarters. 

The company is targeting a user base of 100 million and AUM of over $1 billion by By FY29.

Rohit Garg, Co-founder and CEO, Olyv, said, “As we enter our next phase, we are continuing to expand the breadth of our platform, invest in technology and products, and reach the next billion hardworking and underserved consumers with greater financial access and utility.”

The company has so far raised ~$50 million in equity and ~$150 million in debt, from investors including Fundamentum, SMBC Asia Rising Fund, Lightrock, Unicorn India Ventures, and India SME, as well as reputed family offices, including Gauri Khan’s Family Office, and prominent entrepreneurs and sports personalities.

item.title: Instagram fine-tunes recommendation systems in India to curb sexually suggestive, violent content
item.description: Meta Platforms said on Tuesday that it has fine-tuned Instagram's content recommendation systems in India to curb the visibility of sexually suggestive material and violent content, deploying more advanced artificial intelligence models to identify and filter unwanted posts before they reach users.
item.content:encoded:
Meta Platforms said on Tuesday that it has fine-tuned Instagram's content recommendation systems in India to curb the visibility of sexually suggestive material and violent content, deploying more advanced artificial intelligence models to identify and filter unwanted posts before they reach users.

The India-specific measures apply to content recommended from accounts users do not follow and concern what Instagram's algorithms promote, rather than a blanket ban on the content itself, the company said.

The announcement comes against the backdrop of increased regulatory scrutiny of social media algorithms in India. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, in an October 10 advisory, asked Meta to review its ranking and recommendation systems to ensure potentially misleading, manipulated or out-of-context material is not disproportionately amplified.

Meta, however, did not say if the changes were linked to the government advisory.

The changes have helped halve the frequency with which users report recommended content compared with a year ago, Meta said in a post on its website.

The platform said it had strengthened default protections over the past year, tailoring its systems to content that users in India have said they do not want to see. The measures apply to recommendations across Reels, Explore and Feed, where Instagram surfaces content from accounts users do not already follow.

As part of the upgrades, Instagram is using more capable AI models to assess content directly against its Recommendations Guidelines, enabling its systems to detect and limit potentially objectionable material proactively rather than waiting for users to report or hide it.

"Today, our systems keep more of this content out of recommendations, including sexually suggestive content and content that depicts violence," Meta said.

The company said the improvements had enabled it to proactively reduce the amount of content in India that does not meet its recommendation standards. It did not disclose the absolute volume of content affected, the proportion of recommendations filtered or the methodology used to calculate the decline in user reports.

Instagram's recommendation standards are distinct from its Community Standards, which govern content prohibited on the platform. Material that violates Community Standards is removed, while content that may be objectionable, sensitive or low-quality but does not breach those rules can remain accessible without being recommended to a wider audience. Content unlawful in a particular country is restricted there, the company said.

Recommendations determine how users discover content beyond accounts they actively follow, giving the platform's algorithms considerable influence over what appears in their feeds and is amplified across the service.

Alongside platform-wide recommendation filters, Instagram offers users controls to customise the content they see and manage interactions on the platform.

Its Sensitive Content Control allows users to opt for less sensitive material across Search, Reels, Explore, suggested accounts and in-Feed recommendations. Instagram said its systems in India already exclude the most mature content from recommendations, with the setting allowing users to further limit exposure to other sensitive material.

Users can also choose to see less political content recommended from accounts they do not follow, flag posts through the "Not Interested" option and filter selected words, phrases and emojis from comments and message requests using the Hidden Words feature. Its blocking function prevents specific accounts from finding profiles, viewing posts or sending messages, including through new accounts they may create.

Teenagers receive additional age-appropriate protections through Instagram's Teen Accounts, introduced in India last year. These accounts automatically place younger users in a 13-plus content setting governed by the platform's age-appropriate content guidelines.

The changes come amid growing scrutiny of social media platforms over online safety, algorithm-driven content distribution and the exposure of younger users to potentially harmful material.

Meta said user feedback, including when people hide posts or select "Not Interested", also informs its recommendation systems and helps identify content audiences do not want surfaced to them.

The company said it would continue to refine its detection systems as user behaviour and technology evolve, with feedback from users in India guiding further changes.

item.title: Amazon plans $7B renewable energy investment in India by 2030
item.description: The proposed investment will be over and above the USD 4 billion the company has already contracted in renewable energy projects in India, Amazon said on Tuesday, making it one of the country's largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy.
item.content:encoded:
E-commerce giant Amazon plans to invest an additional $7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, expanding its presence in the country's clean energy market as it seeks to meet growing electricity requirements and reduce the carbon intensity of power used across its operations.

The proposed investment will be over and above the $4 billion the company has already contracted in renewable energy projects in India, Amazon said on Tuesday, making it one of the country's largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy.

The company also announced four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts (MW) across Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. The projects have been secured through power purchase agreements (PPAs) and form part of its existing $4 billion contracted investment portfolio.

The projects comprise a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka, Amazon's largest contracted wind project in Asia to date; a 200 MW hybrid wind and solar project, also in Karnataka; a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh; and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan.

Once operational, Amazon's contracted renewable energy projects in India will have a combined capacity of more than 2 gigawatts (GW), equivalent to the annual electricity requirements of more than 3.5 million Indian households, the company said in a statement.

Amazon did not provide a breakdown of the proposed $7 billion investment, identify the projects it intends to develop under the additional commitment or specify the timeline for deploying the capital beyond its 2030 target.

The investment forms part of a broader global push by Amazon to decarbonise the electricity powering its operations. The company on Tuesday announced a target to reduce the carbon intensity of electricity used across its operations by 65 per cent by 2030, compared with a 2019 baseline.

The target means each unit of electricity consumed by the company would be associated with 65 per cent fewer carbon emissions by the end of the decade. It is part of Amazon's broader Climate Pledge commitment to achieve net-zero carbon emissions across its operations by 2040.

"Our renewable energy investments in India reflect years of sustained effort, planning, and collaboration across the industry. This additional investment of USD 7 billion underlines our long-term commitment, helping bring additional wind and solar capacity online while contributing to India's energy security and long-term renewable energy ambitions," Kara Hurst, Amazon's chief sustainability officer, said.

Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi welcomed the investment, saying it would support India's clean energy ambitions, strengthen energy security and demonstrate growing confidence among global companies in the country's renewable energy sector, according to the statement.

Amazon's Indian renewable energy portfolio currently includes 14 utility-scale wind and solar projects, alongside 43 on-site solar installations across its facilities. Together, the 57 projects are intended to expand carbon-free electricity supply to the grid as well as meet part of the company's operational energy requirements.

Globally, Amazon has contracted more than 700 wind and solar projects with a combined capacity exceeding 40 GW, making it one of the world's largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy.

The company's sustainability investments in India extend to transportation, water management and packaging.

Amazon said it had deployed more than 15,000 electric vehicles across more than 500 Indian cities and was working with Tata Motors to introduce 3,000 electric trucks, which it described as the largest planned electric truck fleet by an e-commerce company in India.

It also said it had achieved water-positive status in India in 2025, ahead of its 2027 target, replenishing more than 120% of the water consumed across its direct operations. Its water replenishment projects, backed by investments exceeding Rs 62 crore, are expected to replenish more than 4 billion litres annually.

In packaging, more than half of Amazon's customer orders in India are shipped in reduced or original packaging, while the company is collaborating with IIT Roorkee to develop alternative packaging materials using agricultural residue.

The renewable energy commitment comes as India seeks to expand non-fossil-fuel electricity generation to meet rising power demand while advancing its longer-term emissions reduction and net-zero objectives. Large corporate power purchase agreements can provide long-term demand visibility for renewable energy developers and support investment in new generation capacity.

item.title: Ola Electric’s dealer-led model reset; Menopause in India’s public health agenda
item.description: The company is betting on a cheaper S1Z scooter and in-house battery manufacturing to win back customers, though the long-term success of its reset depends on retail registrations, supply chain stability, and margin recovery.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

India’s deeptech ecosystem just got a major capital boost. Multi-strategy asset manager Oister Global has launched the Oister Deep Tech Fund, targeting up to Rs 600 crore to back revenue-generating Indian startups. The fund will build a concentrated portfolio of eight to ten mature companies in the frontier tech ecosystem.

Meanwhile, upGrad has launched upGrad Next, a workforce advisory business that will help organisations redesign how they structure, hire, reward and develop employees amid workplace changes due to AI. The move expands upGrad’s corporate offering as it moves beyond skilling into higher education, professional courses, study-abroad services and enterprise learning.

In other news, India’s deeptech companies raised $914 million in 257 rounds in 2025, 34 times the 2016 level. The harder test is turning research and prototypes into commercial products, according to Speciale Invest’s report, India’s Deep Tech Revolution - From the Lab to Growth and Exits.

Edtech companies aren’t the only ones betting big on AI learning. Government programmes are also rapidly expanding India's talent pipeline. According to the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, the Skill India Digital Hub’s SOAR programme now offers 50 AI and AI-application qualifications, drawing over 517,000 enrolments and certifying more than 100,000 learners as of August 2026.

Elsewhere, a new kind of revolution is brewing. About 3.76 crore rural women belonging to self-help groups have achieved Lakhpati Didi status. The Centre’s rural livelihood initiative aims to create 6 crore Lakhpati Didis by March 2029. Additionally, 5.70 crore women have been identified as Potential Lakhpati Didis.

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • Ola Electric’s dealer-led model reset
  • Menopause in India’s public health agenda

Here’s your trivia for today: Which global payments giant began in 1966 when a group of California banks formed the ‘Interbank Card Association’? (Scroll down for the answer)

Analysis

Ola Electric’s dealer-led model reset

EV company Ola Electric is abandoning its direct-to-consumer model and shutting most company-owned showrooms by December 2026 to transition into a dealer-led business. While the broader electric two-wheeler market grew significantly, Ola’s revenue dropped sharply amid severe service backlogs, consumer complaints, and regulatory store closures over missing trade certificates. To recover, Ola rapidly established over 319 dealer outlets, shifting inventory costs to partners and boosting wholesale orders.

Key takeaways:

  • The company is betting on a cheaper S1Z scooter and in-house battery manufacturing to win back customers, though the long-term success of its reset depends on retail registrations, supply chain stability, and margin recovery.
  • The company's Q2 FY27 revenue dropped by 39% to Rs 421 crore even as the wider electric two-wheeler market grew.
  • Between September 2023 and August 2024, the maker of electric two-wheelers received 10,644 complaints through the National Consumer Helpline. Of these, 3,389 concerned service delays and 1,899 were about delayed deliveries, according to media reports.

Health and wellbeing

Menopause in India’s public health agenda

Millions of women in India navigate menopause with little to no support from family or even their healthcare providers. That’s why the Karnataka government’s recent order for a three-month pilot of Ruthu Taare, its Mid-Life Women’s Health and Menopause Programme, in Dakshina district is a welcome step in the right direction.

Key takeaways:

  • The programme will feature dedicated clinics, comprehensive health screenings, mental health assessments, nutrition counselling, and referrals for women aged 35 and above.
  • The pilot will organise dedicated clinic sessions every Wednesday at primary health centres, taluka and district hospitals. Designated medical colleges may organise special clinics on Saturdays.
  • The Ruthu Taare initiative is important because it attempts to bring menopausal care into mainstream conversation and integrate it into public healthcare.

item.title: Fadnavis’ vision for a new Maharashtra: Gen Z, deep tech and $1 trillion
item.description: Devendra Fadnavis on youth in governance, skills over degrees, and his plan to make Maharashtra a trillion-dollar innovation hub.
item.content:encoded:
Few sitting Chief Ministers would spend four to five hours judging student presentations. Devendra Fadnavis did exactly that at the summit of The Governance Challenge (TGC) 2026 in Mumbai, where six finalist teams pitched their answers to one question: what can the Government of Maharashtra do to make the state an innovation hub by 2035?

The challenge drew more than 4,400 three-member teams, over 13,000 students from 30 of India’s leading business and policy schools. After several elimination rounds, six teams presented ideas on healthcare, education, farming and access to credit. The Chief Minister, the 18 finalists and Gaurav Goel, founder & CEO of Samagra, which runs the challenge, then joined Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO at The Bharat Project, YourStory Media for an open conversation.

A government willing to admit it doesn’t have every answer

Fadnavis opened with an unusually candid view of how governments tend to think.

“Normally, in government, we always feel that we know everything, and that we are the ones who will create solutions for every problem. But in my experience of the last 10 years, I feel you need a very fresh perspective to look at every problem.”

The finalists, he said, brought exactly that. They understood technology and how to deploy it, and despite being outsiders to the system, they had clearly thought hard about the problems. Their ideas may not be complete solutions, he added, but they give the government a strong base to build on with its own experience and data.

Why B-schools need a dose of governance

Goel explained that TGC was created to fill a gap in management education. Business school case studies, campus events, internships and placements all lean heavily towards the corporate and startup world, leaving students with little exposure to governance or social impact. TGC tries to change that through immersion, in the hope that the experience stays with students and later draws them towards nation-building.

After the national round, finalists spent two days meeting officials across departments and visiting model schools and primary health centres, while mentors from government and industry helped refine their pitches. The students said the visits upended their assumptions. One admitted that problems look simple from the outside, and that proposing a fix from an air-conditioned room is very different from delivering it on the ground. He was struck by how much infrastructure already exists, including 3D printers in government schools. Others said the competition felt different from the usual hackathons because it pointed towards execution, not just a certificate, and that some teams worked until 3 am refining their ideas.

An 11-year experiment with young talent

For Fadnavis, young people in government is not a new idea. Since 2015, the Chief Minister’s Fellowship, run with IIT Bombay, has placed bright young graduates inside government for a year through a competitive selection process. Some leave jobs at multinationals to join.

One fellowship team built a platform to run and evaluate the state’s farm-pond-on-demand scheme for drought relief and water conservation. The scheme created around 1.5 lakh farm ponds, and the platform won a Prime Minister’s Award. Senior bureaucrats who were sceptical in the early years now compete for fellows, with district collectors asking for two or three at a time.

In 2019, the state also launched a Village Social Transformation initiative with CSR partners across 1,000 villages, asking young people to live in a village for a full year and use CSR funds to fill gaps that rigid government budgets could not. Of 5,000 applicants, roughly 900 to 950 took up the challenge, and not one dropped out.

Goel said Samagra runs on the same belief. Its team of 90 to 100 people has had an average age of 25 to 30 for over a decade. He looks for energy, an impact orientation and raw smarts, and says young recruits are easier to groom because they arrive without baggage.

Experience plus fresh ideas

Fadnavis called Gen Z the first generation born entirely into technology and constantly connected to global best practices. Properly channelled, he said, that exposure produces bright ideas. But he stressed balance: new ideas need mentoring and oversight, and real innovation comes from pairing fresh thinking with experience.

Maharashtra in 2035

Asked what transformation he wants the state to be known for, Fadnavis began with the government machinery itself. Its people, he said, are its most neglected resource, and good work too often depends on an individual minister or officer rather than the institution. Building the state as an institution, with Samagra’s help, is now a priority.

He then set out the economic goal. Maharashtra is a $660 billion economy that he believes can overtake the UAE and Singapore within two years and become India’s first trillion-dollar state economy by 2030. A true welfare state, he argued, must earn before it spends on social programmes. With the state already about 50% urbanised, he wants that urbanisation to drive jobs and sustainable growth.

His vision for 2035 includes a drought-free Maharashtra with water reaching every area, 65% of power from clean sources, and a state that serves as India’s home for startups, frontier technology and deep tech.

Skills over degrees

His advice to students was to stop chasing degrees for their own sake. Future jobs, he said, will depend on the skills people actually acquire. A skilled workforce attracts investment, and investment creates demand for more skilled people. Getting that cycle right would put Maharashtra in a different league.

Innovation for the village

When a student asked what innovation means for a villager with little exposure to technology, Fadnavis gave the line of the day.

“Innovation is a simple solution for a very complex problem. Unless it is a simple solution, it is not an innovation.”

He pointed to the state’s AI advisory tools for farmers and AI models already lifting farm productivity. The problem is that many depend on costly IoT hardware that a farmer with one acre cannot afford. The next round of innovation, he said, must make these tools cheaper and more sustainable.

Purpose first

In closing, Fadnavis told the students that serving the nation does not require a uniform or public office.

Creating jobs, improving livelihoods, lifting people out of poverty and extending healthcare are all forms of service, in any field. Whether they build a startup or chase a unicorn, he urged them to anchor their work in purpose, because purpose matters more than how much they earn.

Shradha called the day a glimpse of what a Viksit Bharat could look like: a Chief Minister who listens, and young people ready to do the work.

item.title: India’s deeptech funding record faces a test of scale: Speciale Invest
item.description: India’s deeptech funding hit $914 million in 2025, but limited growth capital, manufacturing dependencies and weak commercialisation pathways continue to hinder startups from scaling.
item.content:encoded:
India’s deeptech companies raised $914 million in 257 rounds in 2025, 34 times the 2016 level. The harder test is turning research and prototypes into commercial products, notes Speciale Invest’s report, India’s Deep Tech Revolution - From the Lab to Growth and Exits.

Using Tracxn data through August 31 2026, the study covers 8,293 private companies worldwide, including 482 in India. India accounted for 12.8% of deeptech funding rounds in 2025 but received 1.6% of the capital. 

For every 100 seed rounds, India had 23 Series A or B rounds, against 105 globally. Separately, there was one late-stage or private-equity round per 100 Indian seed rounds, against 26 worldwide. Both measures point to funding thinning as companies mature.

Sectoral advantages are uneven. Space firms can tap ISRO testing facilities and suppliers, while life-sciences ventures can draw on India’s pharmaceutical manufacturing base. Private participation in space has widened since 2020 reforms. Registered space startups rose from one in 2014 to about 440 by August 2026. 

In July, Skyroot’s Vikram-I became the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit from Indian soil. It was a milestone, though one launch does not establish a repeatable commercial business. 

The report says battery makers still rely on imported cells and materials. Separately, Exide commissioned phase one of a 6 GWh Bengaluru cell plant in September. Semiconductor developers remain reliant on overseas fabrication and packaging. Semicon 2.0, approved in July with Rs 1,27,500 crore, aims to expand domestic capacity; the first fab is due in 2028.

The six-year Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation Scheme aims to finance high-risk technology. By July 2026, the Technology Development Board had approved 22 projects with Rs 2,192 crore in support. Assistance is mainly through low-interest long-term loans, equity and equity-linked instruments, rather than standard grants.

Turning a successful pilot, or customer trial, into an order remains difficult. Vishesh Rajaram, managing partner at Speciale Invest, said, “Large companies and public-sector buyers can help turn those trials into commercial orders by agreeing upfront on what a pilot must prove and when they’ll make a purchase decision. A first order lets a startup plan production and commit to suppliers.”

Growth capital is smaller too. Indian Series A and B rounds averaged $11.5 million from January to August 2026, against $55.5 million globally, said Vishnu Rajeev, investment partner at Speciale Invest. 

“That gap matters when a founder needs to qualify a product with a major customer or commission a production line before commercial revenue is predictable, Rajeev adds. He argues funding should match milestone costs, with project finance once customers make firm commitments.

The report urges faster funding decisions, shared testing facilities, more domestic Series B and C investors, and plant finance before pilots end. It also considers listings, acquisitions, licensing and secondary share sales as exit routes. 

Deeptech needs not just research funding, but reliable customers and patient growth capital.

item.title: Pragya Misra to lead OpenAI's business development in India and South Asia
item.description: Misra was OpenAI's first hire in India, in 2024. Prior to joining OpenAI, she worked with Truecaller and Meta.
item.content:encoded:
Pragya Misra, OpenAI's head of strategy and global affairs in India, will be taking up a new role where she will be leading the firm's business development for India and South Asia region. 

Announcing the news on Linkedin, she said, "In this new role, I'll focus on building partnerships that help businesses transform with AI, bring our technology to millions more people, and build the infrastructure needed to support this growth," she said.

She also added, "With nearly a fifth of the world’s population, India has a vital role in ensuring AI’s benefits reach more people. In this new role, I’ll focus on building partnerships that help businesses transform with AI, bring our technology to millions more people, and build the infrastructure needed to support this growth.”

Misra was OpenAI's first hire in India, in 2024. Prior to joining OpenAI, she worked with Truecaller and Meta.

This comes at a time when OpenAI has said that India is its largest market. The company had earlier said that it has over 100 million weekly users in India and 1.2 billions users, globally.
